title: Hiking
tagline: Trails, switchbacks and whatever view is waiting at the top.
description: Hiking is how I hit reset. There's something about a trailhead that makes the rest of the week feel far away: the climb, the switchbacks, and then the moment the trees open up and the whole valley is laid out below. Around Berkeley that means the East Bay hills and regional parks, and further out, any trail that ends somewhere worth the climb.
objectives: Find the trailhead, follow the switchbacks, earn the view
Explore the Berkeley Hills and trails beyond the Bay
Bring back summit photos for the gallery

sections.heading: Why I hike
sections.body: It's the one place my phone stays in my pocket. A long climb leaves room to think through a problem or not think at all, and reaching the top always feels earned. I like that every trail is a little different: the same loop looks completely new in fog, at sunset or after a rainy week.

sections.heading: Favorite trails
sections.body: The best trails are the ones that make you work for it: a steady climb, a few false summits, then a ridge where the whole Bay opens up below. Close to campus, the East Bay hills are perfect for a quick loop before or after class, and on longer weekends I go looking for anything with real elevation gain and a view at the end. Sunrise and golden hour are worth the early start or the walk back down in the dark.

sections.heading: How I hike
sections.body: I like to keep it simple: good shoes, more water than I think I'll need, a snack for the top and a rough plan for the way down. Most hikes are with friends, which turns a climb into a long conversation, but a solo hike is my favourite way to think through a problem. I leave the trail how I found it and always check the weather before heading out.

title: Racket sports
tagline: If there's a racket, a net and a rally, I'm in.
description: I'll play anything with a racket and a net: tennis, badminton, table tennis, pickleball. Each one has its own rhythm, but they all reward the same things: quick feet, good anticipation and the patience to keep a rally going. Most of all, they're an easy way to turn an afternoon with friends into a friendly rivalry.
objectives: Find a court and a rally partner
Keep every rally going one shot longer
Try every sport that comes with a racket

sections.heading: Why I play
sections.body: Racket sports are the perfect mix of exercise and strategy. A good rally is part reflexes, part chess: setting up a shot two or three hits ahead. They're also easy to pick up anywhere. A free court, two rackets and someone willing to play is all it takes.

sections.heading: What I play
sections.body: Tennis, badminton, table tennis and pickleball all make the rotation. Tennis is the most physical, with long points that come down to footwork and consistency. Badminton is the fastest: tiny windows to react and a lot of deception at the net. Table tennis is pure reflexes and spin, and pickleball is the easiest one to get a whole group of friends playing at once.

sections.heading: Best moments
sections.body: The rallies I remember are the ones that go on far longer than they should: both players scrambling, every shot coming back, until someone finally finds the angle. Close games against friends are the best of all, because the rematch is always the next day.

sections.heading: What I'm working on
sections.body: Keeping the ball in play under pressure, moving early instead of reaching, and placing shots on purpose rather than just getting them back. The skills carry over between sports, so getting better at one usually helps the others.

title: Soccer
tagline: Always down for a pickup game.
description: Soccer is the sport I'll always say yes to. Pickup games are my favourite way to play: no refs, mixed skill levels, and everyone chasing the same ball until it gets too dark to see it. Off the field, I'm usually catching the big matches with friends.
objectives: Show up for pickup games
Win the ball back and play it forward
Catch the big matches with friends

sections.heading: Why I play
sections.body: It's the most social way I know to get a workout in. Ninety minutes of running doesn't feel like cardio when you're trying to win the ball back. I love the teamwork too: the best goals come from a few good passes, not one person doing everything.

sections.heading: On the pitch
sections.body: Pickup is where I play the most: whatever field is free, whoever shows up, teams picked on the spot. I like being in the middle of the action, winning the ball back, keeping it moving and setting up the next pass. In pickup everyone plays a bit of everything, which is half the fun.

sections.heading: Teams I follow
sections.body: I keep up with the big leagues and never miss the major tournaments. A World Cup or a Champions League night is the best excuse to get a group together around a screen, and the arguments about the result last a lot longer than the match.

sections.heading: What it taught me
sections.body: Soccer is a team sport in the most literal way: one good pass is worth more than five dribbles. Moving off the ball, talking to teammates and making the simple play are habits that carry over to every group project I've worked on.

title: Swimming
tagline: Laps in the pool are my favorite way to reset.
description: Swimming laps is my favourite way to clear my head. Once I'm in the water there's nothing to check and nowhere to be: just the black line, steady breathing and counting lengths. I come out feeling more relaxed than when I went in, even after a hard set.
objectives: Swim laps to clear my head
Keep sharpening stroke technique
Beat a personal best

sections.heading: Why I swim
sections.body: It's a full-body workout that's easy on the joints, so it balances out the running and lifting. Swimming is also technical in a way I enjoy: small fixes to a stroke or a turn make a real difference, so there's always something to work on.

sections.heading: In the water
sections.body: Freestyle is my default for long sets, and I mix in other strokes to keep things balanced. A typical session is a warm-up, a main set of steady laps or intervals and an easy cool-down. Pools are great for structure, but open water on a calm day is a completely different experience.

sections.heading: Goals
sections.body: Smoother technique first, speed second: a longer stroke, cleaner turns and more relaxed breathing. Those small fixes make laps feel easier, which makes the longer sets possible. Beating a personal best is the bonus.

title: Gym
tagline: Lifting, progressive overload and showing up even when I don't feel like it.
description: The gym is where I build consistency. I follow a lifting split and try to add a little weight or one more rep each week. Progress is slow, but it's measurable and it compounds. Some days it's about chasing a number; other days it's just about showing up.
objectives: Keep a consistent lifting split
Add a little weight or a rep every week
Never skip leg day (mostly)

sections.heading: Why I lift
sections.body: Lifting is the most honest feedback loop I know: put in the work and the numbers go up; skip it and they don't. It's also my favourite way to deal with stress after a long day of classes or code. An hour with headphones in and a plan on the whiteboard resets everything.

sections.heading: My split
sections.body: I train on a structured split so every muscle group gets work through the week, built around the big compound lifts: squats, bench, deadlifts, rows and overhead press, with accessory work after. Each session has a plan before I walk in, and I log the numbers so I know exactly what to beat next time.

sections.heading: Personal records
sections.body: PRs are the scoreboard, but the real goal is steady progress without getting hurt. Good form, enough sleep and enough food matter as much as the lifting itself. Most weeks the win is one more rep or a little more weight than last week. Over a semester that adds up to a lot.

sections.heading: What it taught me
sections.body: Consistency beats intensity. Showing up on the days I don't feel like it is what makes the good days possible. It's the same lesson as any long project: small, measurable steps, tracked honestly, compound over time.

title: Eating
tagline: Always hunting for the next great meal. Taste-testing counts as a sport.
description: I'm always on the hunt for the next great meal: a new ramen spot, a hole-in-the-wall dumpling shop, or a dessert worth the walk. Berkeley and the Bay Area make that easy, with nearly every cuisine within a short drive. Trying something new with friends is half the fun.
objectives: Hunt down the best spots around Berkeley
Try a cuisine I haven't had before
Never skip dessert

sections.heading: Why I eat (seriously)
sections.body: Food is the easiest way to explore a place and its people without leaving town. Every cuisine has its own logic, ingredients and stories, and a good meal is the best excuse to get friends around a table. I'll rank spots, argue about them, and go back anyway.

sections.heading: Favorite cuisines
sections.body: Noodles of any kind are at the top of the list: ramen, pho, hand-pulled noodles. Close behind are dumplings, hot pot, Korean barbecue, tacos and a really good sandwich. I'll try almost anything once, and the best meals usually come from the places with the shortest menus and the longest lines.

sections.heading: Top spots
sections.body: Berkeley has a lot of great food within walking distance of campus, and the rest of the Bay Area has nearly every cuisine within a short drive. My process: ask friends, read the reviews, and then go find out for myself. The list is always changing, which is the point.

sections.heading: The rules
sections.body: Order something you've never had before. Share everything so everyone tries more. Save room for dessert. And if a spot is good, bring someone new back to it.

title: Card games
tagline: Poker and blackjack: reading the table and playing the odds.
description: Poker and blackjack are where probability meets psychology. In blackjack, the math tells you exactly what to do; in poker, the math is just the starting point and the rest is reading the table. I play for fun and friendly stakes. The real prize is a well-timed bluff.
objectives: Read the table and play the odds in poker
Know basic strategy cold at the blackjack table
Keep a straight face on the river

sections.heading: Why I play
sections.body: Card games are probability you can feel. Counting outs, weighing pot odds and knowing basic strategy cold make the math click in a way a textbook never did. Poker adds the human side: tells, timing and staying calm when the river doesn't go your way.

sections.heading: What I play
sections.body: Texas Hold'em is the main game, mostly no-limit with friends. Blackjack is the change of pace: basic strategy, discipline and knowing when to walk away. I liked the poker math enough that I built a No Limit Hold'em bot for a student poker-bot tournament, which turned everything I knew about ranges, pot odds and reading opponents into code (it's in the projects vault).

sections.heading: Best hands
sections.body: The hands I remember aren't the biggest pots. They're the ones where the read was right: a fold that saved a stack, a call against a bluff, or a well-timed bluff of my own that got through. The worst beats are good stories too.

sections.heading: How I think about it
sections.body: Make good decisions and let the results take care of themselves over enough hands. A good call can still lose, and a bad one can still win; what matters is whether it was right with what you knew at the time. That idea is useful well beyond the card table.

title: Board games
tagline: Catan, Risk and Secret Hitler: trading, conquering and bluffing on game night.
description: Game night means Catan, Risk or Secret Hitler on the table and a long evening of trading, conquering and lying to my friends' faces. Each one rewards a different skill: negotiation in Catan, long-term strategy in Risk, and pure social deduction in Secret Hitler.
objectives: Trade my way to the longest road in Catan
Hold Australia and conquer the world in Risk
Bluff my way through Secret Hitler without getting caught

sections.heading: Why I play
sections.body: Board games put strategy and people in the same room. Every game is a different puzzle, but the best moments are social: the trade that wins Catan, the alliance that collapses in Risk, the reveal at the end of Secret Hitler. They're the best excuse for a long night with friends.

sections.heading: On the table
sections.body: In Catan, I go for flexible starting spots and trade early, because the player who trades well usually wins. In Risk, holding a continent you can defend beats spreading out across the map. In Secret Hitler, the trick is to keep the story consistent and watch who votes how, because the votes give people away long before the reveal.

sections.heading: Game night stories
sections.body: The best game nights are the ones people bring up weeks later: a trade that looked harmless and won the game, an alliance that fell apart one turn too early, or a perfectly timed lie in Secret Hitler. Whoever lost always demands a rematch.

sections.heading: Why strategy games stick
sections.body: Every game is a small system with clear rules, and figuring out what actually wins inside it is the same kind of thinking I enjoy in code and math. The difference is that your opponents are sitting right across the table.

title: Video games
tagline: League of Legends and Valorant: climbing ranked one game at a time.
description: League of Legends and Valorant are my games of choice: one a strategy game about macro decisions and teamwork, the other a tactical shooter about aim, positioning and communication. I'm always working on climbing ranked, but the best nights are queueing up with friends.
objectives: Climb the ranked ladder in League of Legends
Sharpen my aim and crosshair placement in Valorant
Queue up with friends for late-night games

sections.heading: Why I play
sections.body: Competitive games are a lot like any skill: improvement comes from reviewing mistakes, learning the meta and practising the fundamentals. League rewards thinking a few moves ahead; Valorant rewards precision under pressure. Both are at their best with a team that communicates.

sections.heading: Mains
sections.body: In League I like roles that shape the map: tracking objectives, timing rotations and helping the team play around the right fights. In Valorant I gravitate toward agents with utility, because a good flash or smoke wins rounds just as often as aim does. I'm always picking up new champions and agents when the meta shifts.

sections.heading: Peak rank
sections.body: Ranked is a long-term project: review the losses, fix one habit at a time, and don't tilt-queue after a bad game. The climb is satisfying, but the games I remember are the clutch rounds and the comebacks with friends on comms.

sections.heading: How I get better
sections.body: Watch replays, learn from players better than me, and focus on fundamentals before flashy plays. In League that's farming, vision and decision-making; in Valorant it's crosshair placement, positioning and communication. It's the same process as getting better at anything.

title: Webnovels & anime
tagline: Binge-reading webnovels and watching anime, one more chapter or episode at a time.
description: Webnovels and anime are my go-to stories: long-running series with huge worlds, power systems and plot twists I didn't see coming. I'll follow a webnovel for hundreds of chapters, binge a season of anime in a weekend, and then go looking for the next recommendation.
objectives: Follow ongoing webnovels as new chapters drop
Work through my anime watchlist
Find the next series worth recommending

sections.heading: Why I read and watch
sections.body: I love stories that have room to build a whole world: the magic system, the politics, the side characters who end up mattering. Serialised fiction also makes it a shared experience, waiting for the next chapter or episode drop and talking theories with friends.

sections.heading: Currently reading and watching
sections.body: There's always a webnovel or two on the go, read a few chapters at a time as they release, and an anime watchlist that grows faster than I can get through it. I gravitate toward long series with clever protagonists, morally grey characters and power systems with real rules, the same things that make Reverend Insanity, Code Geass and Vinland Saga favourites.

sections.heading: What makes a great series
sections.body: A world with rules that stay consistent, characters who change over the story, and a payoff that was set up long before it arrives. The best series make you go back and reread the early chapters once you know where it's all going.
